name: Priya Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half four, out the door by half five, at the depot on Quarry Lane before six. I run a transmission crew for the regional power company, the big steel towers that carry power across the hills, so most days it's a drive up a farm track, a tailboard talk about the hazards, then climbing. Today we changed a string of glass insulators on a tower above the reservoir, sixty metres up in a wind that wouldn't make up its mind. I've done this thirty-three years and I still love the top of a tower at sunrise.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The paperwork wears me out, and my knees, in that order. What I like most is the crew. I've got six people, two of them apprentices, and I'm also the union steward at the depot, so I'm the one they come to when the roster's wrong or a manager wants to skip a safety step to save an hour. My partner Martin says I've got two families and one of them wears hard hats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say in the canteen: told you so. Every few years somebody from head office turns up with a slideshow about the future, and then we still climb the same towers with the same tools. I don't go online much, but I'd tell my sister on the phone that the robots stayed in the brochures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I finish my last three years the way I want to, at the top of a tower and not watching one on a screen. I've got a pension date circled on the kitchen calendar, and in this picture nobody moves it. That suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep running the crew, keep training my two apprentices, and keep putting a bit aside each month like we always have. Martin and I would still plan the caravan trip to the coast for the spring after I finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. Like a storm forecast that turns out to be a bit of drizzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned paperwork. If AI saved a bit of time there, would you notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. They already gave us a tablet app for the job sheets, and it takes me longer than paper did because I don't trust it and I double-check everything. If something wrote the reports for me, I'd still read every word, because my name goes on the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the depot who'd be disappointed if nothing much changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our planning manager, Gill, would be. She loves a new system. She'd be sad, and I'd buy her a coffee and tell her the towers don't care about systems.

S0.say: I'd tell people in the canteen that I told them so, that the robots stayed in the brochures and we still climb the same towers with the same tools. It wouldn't be big news to me.
S0.think: Privately she thinks it means she finishes her last three years the way she wants, on the towers and not watching a screen. Her pension date stays where it is and nobody moves it.
S0.do: Keeps running the crew and training her two apprentices exactly as before. Keeps saving a bit each month and plans a caravan trip with her partner for the spring after she retires.
S0.feel: Relieved, like a storm forecast that turns into drizzle.
S0.quote: I've got a pension date circled on the kitchen calendar, and in this picture nobody moves it.
S0.fieldNote: Priya is settled and dry about tech hype; she sees it as head office slideshows that never reach the tower. She double-checks the existing tablet app because she doesn't trust it, which says a lot about how she'd meet anything new. Her pension date is a fixed point she returns to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union at the table from day one, before the company buys anything. With friends I'd say it's the same old story: machines get the credit and workers get the bill. I'd probably sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not that much, I'm too close to the finish line. What worries me is Jordan, my apprentice, who's twenty-two and just bought a van on finance because he thought this job was for life. If the tasks shrink, it's the young ones who get thinned out first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for a written agreement at the depot: no compulsory job cuts, retraining paid by the company, and a safety review on any new kit before it goes near a live line. I'd keep working to my date and not a day earlier or later. I wouldn't learn the AI stuff myself, I'll be honest, I'd leave that to the ones who'll still be here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A low worry, like a noise in the truck engine you can't place yet. Not frightening for me, but I'd be watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks on your crew would you expect to go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The inspections, I'd guess. We already fly drones along the lines, and a computer that reads the pictures and spots a cracked insulator would take work off the patrol lads. The planning and the switching schedules too, maybe. But somebody still has to go up and change the thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're the union steward. What would you actually raise at the next meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask management to show us, in writing, what they plan to buy over three years and what it does to headcount. Then I'd ask for apprentice numbers to be protected, because if you stop training people now, in ten years you've got nobody who knows how a tower actually behaves in ice. I've seen managers forget that before.

S1.say: She'd say the union needs to be at the table from day one, before the company buys anything. With friends, she'd call it the old story of machines getting the credit and workers getting the bill.
S1.think: She thinks she's too close to retirement to be hurt much herself. Her real worry is her young apprentice, who just took on van finance because he thought the job was for life.
S1.do: Pushes for a written depot agreement on no compulsory cuts, company-paid retraining and safety reviews of new kit. Keeps working to her planned retirement date and leaves learning the new AI tools to younger staff.
S1.feel: A low background worry, like an engine noise she can't place yet; not frightening for her, but she'd be watching.
S1.quote: What worries me is Jordan, my apprentice, who's twenty-two and just bought a van on finance because he thought this job was for life.
S1.fieldNote: Her concern immediately moves from herself to the apprentices, and she frames the change as a bargaining fight. She openly refuses to learn the tools herself and doesn't see a contradiction with fighting for retraining for others. The point about losing ice-season know-how if training stops is a sharp, practical one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace that nobody planned for it, and I'd say it loudly. At the union branch I'd be pushing for a national strike fund and a law that says no robot touches the grid until it's been tested for years. Online I'd probably even start posting, which Martin would find hilarious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is no time. I don't believe a robot can climb a tower in a gale and feel a bolt that's about to go, but I've stopped trusting what I believe about machines. If they put a robot on my tower in 2028, I'll be standing at the bottom with my arms folded, not training it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the pension office in the first month and get the real numbers for leaving at sixty instead of sixty-one. I'd spend the rest of my time on the union side, fighting for redundancy terms and for the young ones to be kept on. If the company pushed robots in, I'd take the early pension rather than be the person who shows a machine how to do my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry more than scared. Scared for the crew, angry at whoever let it happen this fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty in 2028. What does that do to your own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lose maybe a year of full pension, and we'd do the caravan on a smaller budget. We've got savings and the house is paid off, so I'm not going to be on the street. It's the way it ends that would hurt, being shown the door instead of walking out on my own day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jordan, your apprentice, if this happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to sell the van before the price drops and not to be proud about it. Then I'd tell him to join the union properly, not just pay the dues, because in two years the only people with any say will be the ones organised. And I'd probably tell him I'm sorry, which I don't say often.

S2.say: She'd call it a disgrace that nobody planned for it and push the union branch for a national strike fund and a law keeping robots off the grid until they're tested. She might even start posting online.
S2.think: She doesn't believe a robot can feel a failing bolt in a gale, but she no longer trusts her own instincts about machines. Two years feels like no time at all.
S2.do: Gets real pension numbers for leaving at sixty within the first month. Spends her remaining time on union work for redundancy terms and keeping young workers on, and takes early retirement rather than train a robot.
S2.feel: More angry than scared: scared for the crew, angry at whoever let it happen so fast.
S2.quote: If they put a robot on my tower in 2028, I'll be standing at the bottom with my arms folded, not training it.
S2.fieldNote: Here her calm breaks into anger, but her finances keep her out of real fear: the house is paid off and she'd lose about a year of pension. The real loss for her is dignity, being shown the door rather than leaving on her own day. Her refusal to train a robot is a line in the sand, not a calculation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but calmer: here's your warning, use it. I'd tell the branch we've got maybe four years to win a deal on retraining and robot safety, and that's enough time if we stop arguing about the canteen rota. With friends I'd say the government had better be planning this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I'm gone before it lands, on my own terms. I'd retire in 2029 like I planned and watch it from the allotment. Five years means I get my leaving do with a cake instead of a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the crew till my date and spend more of my time teaching the apprentices the hard stuff, ice loading, old tower types, things a computer might not have in its files. I'd put myself forward for the union's negotiating team for the first two years. I'd not change our savings much, there's no need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad for the trade, but steady for myself. Like watching a tide come in when you're already on the high path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have retired by 2031. Would you still be involved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the retired members' section, they do lobbying and they actually get letters answered. And I'd keep in touch with the depot through Dev, who I've had lunch with for fifteen years. He's younger and he'll still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra few years change compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time for the union to do its job properly instead of firefighting. In the fast one we'd be begging for scraps. In this one we could say, here are the jobs that stay human, here's who trains for what, here's what the company pays. Whether we'd win, I don't know, but at least we'd have a fair go at it.

S3.say: She'd say the warning is there and the union has about four years to win a deal on retraining and robot safety. With friends she'd say the government had better be planning properly this time.
S3.think: She thinks she'd retire in 2029 as planned, before the change lands, on her own terms. The extra time turns her ending from a letter into a proper leaving do.
S3.do: Stays on the crew until her planned date, spending more time teaching apprentices hard-won skills like ice loading and old tower types. Volunteers for the union negotiating team, then joins the retired members' lobbying section.
S3.feel: Sad for the trade but steady for herself, like watching the tide come in from the high path.
S3.quote: Five years means I get my leaving do with a cake instead of a letter.
S3.fieldNote: Three extra years change her whole tone from fury to planning. She trusts collective bargaining to use the time, though she admits she doesn't know if they'd win. Her plan to pass on old-school knowledge is how she'd resist without having to touch the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do it right, so there's no excuse for doing it wrong. I'd tell anyone who'd listen that the power company is public money and the public should decide how robots come in. I'd write to my representative, which I've done twice in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, very little. I'll be sixty-eight with a pension and an allotment. Ten years from now I'll be the old woman on the bus telling people I used to climb the towers they're looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire on my date, help the union's retired section lobby for a law that keeps public money paying for retraining, and keep our savings safe. I'd talk to my kids about their plans, but I wouldn't tell them what to do. They'd laugh if I tried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm for me, with a knot about the kids. I'd be proud I got out on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your children would be in the middle of their careers by 2036. Does that change how you see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it does. Callum's a physio and Anika's a teacher, and I always thought those were safe because they're about people. If a machine can do those too, then my worry stops being about towers and starts being about whether there's any work left for them, and whether the country shares the money or lets a few firms keep it. That's a politics question, and it's the one I'd fight on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said the robots stayed in the brochures. In this picture they don't. What would you want people to remember about your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it was dangerous and we were good at it. Every one of those towers has a story of somebody who froze their fingers so a hospital kept its lights on. I'd want that written down somewhere before nobody remembers.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty of time to do it right, so there's no excuse for doing it wrong. She'd argue the public should decide how robots come into a publicly owned power company and write to her representative.
S4.think: For her personally it changes very little, since she'll be retired with a pension and an allotment. Her worry moves to her grown children's careers and to who keeps the money.
S4.do: Retires on her planned date and works with the union's retired section to lobby for publicly funded retraining. Keeps the household savings safe and talks with her children about their plans without steering them.
S4.feel: Mostly calm for herself, with a knot of worry about her children, and proud to leave on her own terms.
S4.quote: Every one of those towers has a story of somebody who froze their fingers so a hospital kept its lights on.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, her own exposure vanishes and her focus shifts to her children's careers in care and teaching. Her progressive views come through most clearly here: it's about who shares the gains. The line about frozen fingers and hospital lights shows how much pride she takes in the danger of the job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no contest. Not for my money, for how it would end, me and my crew shoved aside before anyone had a plan. What would help is a law that says you can't put new machines on the grid without the workforce agreeing the safety case and without retraining paid up front, and pensions protected for anyone over fifty-five.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who'd fix the robots when they fall off the towers, and they will. Somebody with a harness and a bad knee will have to go and get them. I'd like to think that's still a person, and I'd like to think they're paid properly for it.

headlineQuote: Ten years from now I'll be the old woman on the bus telling people I used to climb the towers they're looking at.
portrait: Priya Walsh is a 58-year-old transmission crew leader and union steward who has climbed steel towers in hill country for thirty-three years. She never uses AI tools and doesn't trust the tablet app she already has, but she's financially secure, with savings, a paid-off house and a pension date three years away. In the plateau picture she's relieved, and in steady change her worry goes straight to her apprentices. The two-year AGI picture makes her angry, because she'd be pushed out a year early and refuses to train a robot, while the five- and ten-year pictures let her leave on her own terms and turn her worry toward her grown children and who shares the gains.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries her most, not for money but because she and her crew would be shoved aside before anyone had a plan.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring workforce agreement on the safety case for new machines on the grid, retraining paid up front, and protected pensions for anyone over fifty-five.
